question: Should doctors taper patients off long-term opioids when their pain has been stable on the same dose?
answer: Long-term opioids have never been shown to keep relieving chronic pain beyond a few months, while overdose risk climbs with dose and tolerance builds. A patient stable on a high dose still carries that risk every day. Slow, agreed tapers let some patients discover their pain is no worse without the drug.
move: Whichever side you took, weigh the risk of stopping against the risk of staying.
ask: When I stop a long habit, have I weighed the risk of stopping against the risk of staying?
counterpoint: Tapering is not neutral. In a 2021 study of over 100,000 US patients on stable long-term opioids, those tapered had about 68% more overdoses and more than twice the mental-health crises of those kept on their dose. A patient pushed off a drug they depend on may turn to street supply, which is far deadlier.
reference: Agnoli et al., Association of Dose Tapering With Overdose or Mental Health Crisis Among Patients Prescribed Long-term Opioids, JAMA, 2021
